moments.title: A paper started in a kitchen
moments.text: Robert S. Abbott printed the first Chicago Defender, a run of about 300 copies, working out of a small kitchen in his landlord's apartment. Abbott later struck a deal with Pullman porters to carry the paper across the South, where copies were passed hand to hand and read in barbershops; its calls to come north helped drive the Great Migration.

moments.title: A home on Indiana Ave
moments.text: The Defender moved its offices and presses into a former synagogue at 3435 S. Indiana Ave, built in 1899 to a design by Henry L. Newhouse. It stayed until 1960.

moments.title: Named a Chicago Landmark
moments.text: The building was designated as part of the Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District.

moments.title: The print edition ends
moments.text: The Defender ended its print edition after 114 years.

moments.title: Today: the former Defender building
moments.text: The landmark building on Indiana Ave in Bronzeville, sold in 2021, still stands.

checked.notes: Founded May 5, 1905 (PBS, Wikipedia; BlackPast says May 6, 300 copies). The story's 'landlady's kitchen' was changed: MLB.com says a small kitchen in his landlord's apartment. Pullman porter distribution and the Great Migration role per Britannica; no single date is given, so it is folded into the founding moment. 3435 S. Indiana: 1899 synagogue by Henry L. Newhouse, Defender home 1920 to 1960, Chicago Landmark Sept 9, 1998 (Chicago Landmarks, Wikipedia). Print edition ended 2019 (NMAAHC). Sold 2021 for $2.48 million.
